01 From second.pdf and first.pdf

The whole system, end to end

Before any formula, you need the map. Every other module in this course is a zoom-in on one box of the diagram below.

1.1 What problem are we even solving?

Somebody wants to send something — a voice, a photo, a video, a sensor reading — to somebody far away. Between them is a channel: air, a copper cable, an optical fibre, or space. The channel is not kind. It weakens the signal, it adds noise, it bends the signal out of shape, and other people's signals crash into yours.

So the goal of a digital communication system is written in one line at the end of your second.pdf:

The one-line goal

Send information reliably (very few mistakes) and efficiently (fast, and without wasting bandwidth or battery) across a noisy channel.

Everything else — entropy, Huffman coding, Hamming codes, Viterbi decoding — is just a tool for hitting those two words: reliably and efficiently.

Why go digital at all?

An analog signal that is damaged stays damaged, and every amplifier along the way makes it a bit worse. A digital signal is only ever a 0 or a 1. As long as the noise is not big enough to flip a 0 into a 1, the receiver can rebuild the signal perfectly. And because it is only 0s and 1s, we can do clever things to it: compress it, encrypt it, and add error-correcting maths. You cannot do any of that easily with an analog waveform.

1.2 The block diagram you must be able to draw

This is the diagram in your second.pdf. It is worth 10–15 marks on its own, so learn to draw it from memory.

Your ninth.pdf draws the same link in a simpler form — the version used when we are studying baseband transmission, so the modulator is replaced by a line code encoder and the channel coding stage is left out.

1.3 What each block actually does

Take them one at a time. This is the vocabulary for the rest of the course.

Information source
The thing making the message: a microphone, a camera, a keyboard, a temperature sensor.
A/D converter (analog to digital)
Turns a smooth real-world wave into numbers. Three steps: sampling (take readings at regular times), quantization (round each reading to the nearest allowed level), encoding (write each level as a binary number). This whole block is Module 2.
Source encoder
Squeezes the data. It removes the parts that are repeated or predictable, so fewer bits are needed. This is compression. Think ZIP, JPEG, MP3. This is Module 7.
Channel encoder (FEC)
Adds extra bits back — but not random extra bits. Carefully designed extra bits that let the receiver spot and repair errors caused by noise. This is Module 8.
Interleaver
Optional. It shuffles the order of the bits before sending. If the channel then wipes out a whole burst of neighbouring bits, un-shuffling at the far end spreads that damage thinly across many codewords, and error correction can handle thin damage far better than one big hole.
Digital modulator
Turns groups of bits into actual electrical waveforms (called symbols) that can travel. Examples from your syllabus: BPSK, QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM, 256-QAM.
Up-converter and RF amplifier
Shifts the signal up to the radio frequency that the antenna can radiate, and makes it powerful enough to survive the journey.
Channel
Air, cable, fibre, satellite link. Where all the damage happens.
LNA and down-converter
LNA = Low Noise Amplifier. The received signal is tiny, so it must be amplified before anything else — and by an amplifier that adds as little noise of its own as possible. Then the signal is shifted back down from radio frequency.
Demodulator / detector
Looks at the received waveform and decides: was that symbol a 0 or a 1 (or which of the 16 QAM points)? This is a guess, and sometimes the guess is wrong. That is where bit errors are born.
Channel decoder
Uses the extra bits the channel encoder added to find and fix the wrong guesses.
Source decoder
Un-squeezes the compressed data back to full size.
D/A converter
Turns the numbers back into a smooth wave for the speaker or screen.
Exam tip

Examiners love this question: “Source coding removes redundancy but channel coding adds redundancy. Is this not a contradiction?”

Answer: No. Source coding removes useless, uncontrolled redundancy that was already sitting in the data by accident. Channel coding then adds back a small amount of useful, carefully designed redundancy that is mathematically built to fight noise. You throw out the junk, then add the right tool.

1.4 How we score a system

Four numbers decide whether a design is good. These appear in your second.pdf and again in Module 8.

Formula — performance measures
BER=number of bits received wronglytotal number of bits sent\mathrm{BER} = \frac{\text{number of}\, \mathrm{bits}\, \text{received wrongly}}{\text{total number of}\, \mathrm{bits}\, \text{sent}}BER=total number ofbitssentnumber ofbitsreceived wrongly​
SER=number of symbols received wronglytotal symbols sent\mathrm{SER} = \frac{\text{number of}\, \mathrm{symbols}\, \text{received wrongly}}{\text{total}\, \mathrm{symbols}\, \text{sent}}SER=totalsymbolssentnumber ofsymbolsreceived wrongly​
SNR=signal powernoise power→often written as EbN0\mathrm{SNR} = \frac{\text{signal power}}{\text{noise power}} \to \frac{\text{often written as}\, E_{b}}{N_{0}}SNR=noise powersignal power​→N0​often written asEb​​
SNRdB=10log⁡10(EbN0)\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}} = 10 \log_{10}\left( \frac{E_{b}}{N_{0}} \right)SNRdB​=10log10​(N0​Eb​​)
In simple words

BER (Bit Error Rate) is your report card. A BER of 10−6 means one bit in a million comes out wrong. Lower is better.

Eb is the energy spent on one bit. N0 is the noise power in each hertz of bandwidth. So Eb/N0 asks: how loud is one bit compared to the hiss? Louder means fewer mistakes, so higher Eb/N0 always gives lower BER.

We write it in dB because these numbers span a huge range. The formula 10 log10(…) squashes a range of millions into a comfortable range of about 0 to 60.

What can you change to improve BER? Your PDF lists five levers: the modulation scheme, the bandwidth, the Eb/N0, the coding technique, and the channel conditions. Only the first four are under your control.

1.5 What is AWGN?

You will see “AWGN” on nearly every slide and in every unit heading of your syllabus. Break the four letters apart:

  • A — Additive. The noise simply adds to your signal: y(t) = x(t) + n(t). It does not multiply or twist it.
  • W — White. Like white light contains all colours, this noise contains all frequencies equally. Its power is spread flat across the whole spectrum.
  • G — Gaussian. The noise voltage at any instant follows the bell curve. Small values are common, huge values are rare.
  • N — Noise. Unwanted random electrical energy, mostly from the random jiggling of electrons because of heat.

So an AWGN channel is the simplest useful model of a real channel: your signal, plus flat random bell-curve hiss. It is the standard baseline that every textbook uses.

1.6 Where in the spectrum does all this live?

Your first.pdf is a map of the electromagnetic spectrum. You do not need to memorise every number, but you should know the order and roughly where the famous systems sit.

Spectrum, from lowest frequency to highest
BandFrequencyUsed for
Radio waves105–109 HzAM/FM radio, TV, maritime and aviation VHF
  → FM broadcast88–108 MHzCar radio
  → Mobile 2G/3G/4G700 MHz–2.6 GHzPhone calls, mobile data
  → 5G sub-63–7 GHzMain 5G coverage layer
Microwaves~1011 HzSatellite links, radar, backhaul, 5G mmWave (24–100 GHz)
Terahertz100 GHz–3 THz6G research
Infrared~1013 HzTV remotes, optical fibre
Visible light~1015 HzLi-Fi / visible light communication
Ultraviolet~1017 HzResearch
X-rays~1021 HzImaging, research

In simple words

Higher frequency gives you more bandwidth, so more data per second. But higher frequency also travels a shorter distance and is blocked more easily by walls, rain and even leaves. That is the eternal trade: 5G mmWave is blisteringly fast but only works across a street; 700 MHz is slower but covers a whole town.

Your first.pdf also lists where this is going: smart cities, self-driving cars, industrial IoT, remote surgery, AR/VR, holographic calls, drones, low-orbit satellite internet, quantum communication and AI-managed networks. All of them need more bits per second, more reliably — which is exactly what the rest of this course is about.

02 From seventh.pdf — Tutorial 3

Sampling, quantization and PCM

This is the A/D block of Module 1, opened up. It is also the single most exam-heavy numerical topic in your materials — a whole tutorial is devoted to it.

2.1 The three steps of PCM

PCM stands for Pulse Code Modulation. It is the standard recipe for turning a smooth analog signal into bits. It has exactly three steps, and you must be able to name them:

  1. Sampling — measure the signal's height at regular time intervals.
  2. Quantization — round each measured height to the nearest allowed level.
  3. Encoding — write each level number as a binary codeword.

2.2 Step 1 — Sampling and the Nyquist rule

How often must you measure? If you measure too rarely, you miss the fast wiggles and the rebuilt signal is wrong — a fault called aliasing. The answer is the most famous rule in the subject:

Formula — Nyquist sampling criterion
fs≥2fmf_{s} \ge 2 f_{m}fs​≥2fm​

fs = sampling frequency (samples per second)  ·  fm = highest frequency present in the signal (Hz)

The value 2 fm is called the Nyquist rate. Sampling exactly at it is the minimum; sampling above it is safer.

In simple words

You must take at least two samples in every cycle of the fastest wiggle in your signal. One sample to catch the peak, one to catch the trough. Fewer than two and a fast wave can pretend to be a slow wave, and you can never tell them apart afterwards.

Example: human speech on a telephone is limited to about 4 kHz, so telephones sample at 8 000 times a second. Music goes up to 20 kHz, so CDs sample at 44 100 times a second — slightly above 2 × 20 kHz, to leave room for the filter.

2.3 Step 2 — Quantization

A sample's true height could be any number at all: 2.718281828… volts. We cannot store infinite digits, so we allow only L fixed levels and round to the nearest one. The rounding error we accept is called quantization noise.

Formula — levels, bits and step size

n = log2 L   (bits per sample)    or equivalently    L = 2n

Δ=Vpeak−to−peak2nstep size, volts\begin{aligned} \Delta &= \frac{V_{\text{peak} - \quad\text{to}\quad - \text{peak}}}{2^{n}} && \text{step size, volts} \end{aligned}Δ​=2nVpeak−to−peak​​​​step size, volts​
Pq=Δ212quantization noise power\begin{aligned} P_{q} &= \frac{\Delta^{2}}{12} \\ &\quad \text{quantization noise power} \end{aligned}Pq​​=12Δ2​quantization noise power​
ϵmax⁡=Δ2largest possible rounding error\begin{aligned} \epsilon_{\max} &= \frac{\Delta}{2} \\ &\quad \text{largest possible rounding error} \end{aligned}ϵmax​​=2Δ​largest possible rounding error​
In simple words

Δ (say “delta”) is the height of one step on the ladder. Take the full voltage range of the signal and cut it into 2n equal slices — each slice is Δ tall.

Because you always round to the nearest level, the worst you can ever be wrong is half a step, which is why εmax = Δ/2.

The Δ2/12 comes from statistics: if the error is equally likely to be anywhere between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2, its average power works out to exactly Δ2/12. Just memorise it — the derivation is not asked.

Signal-to-quantization-noise ratio

This is the number that says how good your quantizer is. There are two forms and you need both.

Formula — SQNR, both forms

General:   SNR = Vrms2 ÷ (Δ2/12)   = signal power ÷ quantization noise power

Full-scale sine wave only:  SQNRdB≈6.02n+1.76\begin{aligned} \text{Full-scale sine wave only}:\; \mathrm{SQNR}_{\mathrm{dB}} &\approx 6.02 n + 1.76 \end{aligned}Full-scale sine wave only:SQNRdB​​≈6.02n+1.76​
Exam tip — which form to use

Use 6.02n + 1.76 only when the question says the signal is a sine wave filling the whole range (“full-scale sinusoidal”). That is Tutorial 3 Question 1.

Use Vrms2 ÷ (Δ2/12) whenever the question gives you an actual Vrms value. That is Tutorial 3 Question 2. Using the wrong one is the most common mistake in this topic.

Remember the headline: every extra bit buys you about 6 dB. Double the number of levels, and quantization noise drops by 6 dB.

2.4 Step 3 — Encoding, bit rate and bandwidth

Formula — PCM bit rate and transmission bandwidth
Rb=n×fsbits per second\begin{aligned} R_{b} &= n \times f_{s} && \text{bits per second} \end{aligned}Rb​​=n×fs​​​bits per second​
Polar NRZ:  BT≈Rb2\begin{aligned} \text{Polar NRZ}:\; B_{T} &\approx \frac{R_{b}}{2} \end{aligned}Polar NRZ:BT​​≈2Rb​​​
RZ:  BT≈Rb\begin{aligned} \text{RZ}:\; B_{T} &\approx R_{b} \end{aligned}RZ:BT​​≈Rb​​
In simple words

Bit rate is simply how many samples per second multiplied by how many bits each sample costs. Nothing clever.

The bandwidth rules say: an RZ pulse is only half a bit wide, so it wiggles twice as fast, so it needs twice the bandwidth of NRZ. You will meet RZ and NRZ properly in Module 3.

2.5 Worked example — Tutorial 3, Question 1

Worked example — TV signal

Question. A television signal having a bandwidth of 4.2 MHz is transmitted using a binary PCM system. The number of quantization levels is 512. Determine (1) code word length, (2) bit rate, (3) transmission bandwidth, (4) signal-to-quantization-noise ratio.

  1. Write down what you are given
    fm=4.2 MHz⋅L=512f_{m} = 4.2\, \mathrm{MHz} \cdot L = 512fm​=4.2MHz⋅L=512
  2. Find the sampling frequency (Nyquist)
    fs=2fm=2×4.2 MHzf_{s} = 2 f_{m} = 2 \times 4.2\, \mathrm{MHz}fs​=2fm​=2×4.2MHz

    fs = 8.4 MSamples/sec

  3. Find the code word length

    Ask: 2 to what power gives 512? Since 512 = 29:

    n=log⁡2L=log⁡2512=9n = \log_{2} L = \log_{2} 512 = 9n=log2​L=log2​512=9

    n = 9 bits/sample

  4. Find the bit rate
    Rb=n×fs=9×8.4×106R_{b} = n \times f_{s} = 9 \times 8.4 \times 10^{6}Rb​=n×fs​=9×8.4×106

    Rb = 75.6 Mb/s

  5. Find the transmission bandwidth — give both cases
    Polar NRZ:  BT≈Rb2=75.62\begin{aligned} \text{Polar NRZ}:\; B_{T} &\approx \frac{R_{b}}{2} = \frac{75.6}{2} \end{aligned}Polar NRZ:BT​​≈2Rb​​=275.6​​

    BT (NRZ) ≈ 37.8 MHz

    RZ:  BT≈Rb\begin{aligned} \text{RZ}:\; B_{T} &\approx R_{b} \end{aligned}RZ:BT​​≈Rb​​

    BT (RZ) ≈ 75.6 MHz

  6. Find the SQNR

    No Vrms is given, and we assume a full-scale sine wave, so use the 6.02n rule:

    SQNRdB=6.02n+1.76=6.02(9)+1.76=54.18+1.76\mathrm{SQNR}_{\mathrm{dB}} = 6.02 n + 1.76 = 6.02 (9) + 1.76 = 54.18 + 1.76SQNRdB​=6.02n+1.76=6.02(9)+1.76=54.18+1.76

    SQNR ≈ 55.94 dB ≈ 56 dB

2.6 Worked example — Tutorial 3, Question 2

This one runs backwards. The channel speed is fixed, and you must work out how many bits per sample you are allowed to afford.

Worked example — fitting PCM into a 50 kbit/s channel

Question. A signal of bandwidth 3.5 kHz is sampled, quantized and coded by a PCM system. The coded signal is transmitted over a channel supporting a transmission rate of 50 kbits/sec. Determine the maximum signal-to-noise ratio obtainable. The input signal has Vpeak-to-peak = 4 V and Vrms = 0.2 V.

  1. Write down what you are given
    fm=3.5 kHz⋅Rb=50 kbits⋅Vpp=4V⋅Vrms=0.2Vf_{m} = 3.5\, \mathrm{kHz} \cdot R_{b} = \frac{50\, \text{kbit}}{s} \cdot V_{pp} = 4 V \cdot V_{\text{rms}} = 0.2 Vfm​=3.5kHz⋅Rb​=s50kbit​⋅Vpp​=4V⋅Vrms​=0.2V
  2. Find the minimum sampling rate
    fs=2fm=2×3.5 kHzf_{s} = 2 f_{m} = 2 \times 3.5\, \mathrm{kHz}fs​=2fm​=2×3.5kHz

    fs = 7 kSamples/sec

  3. Find how many bits per sample the channel can afford

    Rearrange Rb = n fs to get n:

    nmax⁡=Rbfs=50⋅0007000=7.142n_{\max} = \frac{R_{b}}{f_{s}} = \frac{50 \cdot 000}{7} 000 = 7.142nmax​=fs​Rb​​=750⋅000​000=7.142

    Bits must be a whole number, and we must not exceed the channel rate, so round down:

    n = 7 bits/sample

  4. Find the step size
    Δ=Vpp2n=427=4128\Delta = \frac{V_{pp}}{2^{n}} = \frac{4}{2^{7}} = \frac{4}{128}Δ=2nVpp​​=274​=1284​

    Δ = 0.03125 V

  5. Find SNR as a plain ratio

    Here Vrms is given, so use the general form:

    SNR=Vrms2Δ212=(0.2)2(0.03125)212\mathrm{SNR} = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}^{2}}{\frac{\Delta^{2}}{12}} = \frac{(0.2)^{2}}{\frac{(0.03125)^{2}}{12}}SNR=12Δ2​Vrms2​​=12(0.03125)2​(0.2)2​
    =0.040.000976612=0.040.00008138= \frac{0.04}{\frac{0.0009766}{12}} = \frac{0.04}{0.00008138}=120.0009766​0.04​=0.000081380.04​

    SNR = 491.52

  6. Convert to decibels
    SNRdB=10log⁡10(491.52)\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{dB}} = 10 \log_{10}(491.52)SNRdB​=10log10​(491.52)

    SNRmax = 26.91 dB

Why is this only 27 dB when Question 1 gave 56 dB? Because here the signal is quiet. A full-scale sine wave with Vpp = 4 V would have Vrms = 2/√2 ≈ 1.414 V, but this signal's Vrms is only 0.2 V — about seven times smaller. A quiet signal sits closer to the quantization noise floor, so the ratio is worse. This is exactly why real systems use companding (μ-law and A-law).

2.7 Time Division Multiplexing, and the full-pipeline example

TDM means many signals share one wire by taking turns. Signal 1 sends a sample, then signal 2 sends a sample, then signal 3, and so on; after the last one it goes back to signal 1. If you have N signals each sampled at fs, the shared line must carry N × fs samples per second.

Formula — TDM aggregate bit rate
Rb=N×fs×nR_{b} = N \times f_{s} \times nRb​=N×fs​×n

N = number of multiplexed channels  ·  fs = samples/sec per channel  ·  n = bits/sample

The next example is the biggest in your materials. It chains together sampling, quantization, TDM and raised-cosine bandwidth (which is Module 3). Do it now, and revisit it after Module 3.

Worked example — Tutorial 2, Example 5 (telemetry system)

Question. In a certain telemetry system, eight message signals having 2 kHz bandwidth each are time-division multiplexed using a binary PCM technique. The error in sampling amplitude cannot be greater than 1 percent of the peak amplitude. Determine the minimum transmission bandwidth required if raised-cosine pulses with roll-off factor α = 0.2 are used. The sampling rate must be at least 25 percent above the Nyquist rate.

  1. Sampling rate per channel
    Nyquist rate=2B=2×2 kHz=4 kHz\text{Nyquist rate} = 2 B = 2 \times 2\, \mathrm{kHz} = 4\, \mathrm{kHz}Nyquist rate=2B=2×2kHz=4kHz

    “At least 25% above Nyquist” means multiply by 1.25:

    fs=1.25×4 kHzf_{s} = 1.25 \times 4\, \mathrm{kHz}fs​=1.25×4kHz

    fs = 5 kHz per channel

  2. Turn the 1% error rule into a number of levels

    The largest rounding error is half a step, and it must stay under 1% of the peak amplitude A:

    Δ2≤0.01A\frac{\Delta}{2} \le 0.01 A2Δ​≤0.01A

    For a uniform quantizer covering the range −A to +A, the full range is 2A, so Δ = 2A/L. Substituting:

    2A2L≤0.01A⇒AL≤0.01A⇒L≥100\frac{2 A}{2 L} \le 0.01 A \Rightarrow \frac{A}{L} \le 0.01 A \Rightarrow L \ge 1002L2A​≤0.01A⇒LA​≤0.01A⇒L≥100
  3. Turn levels into bits

    We need at least 100 levels, and levels must be a power of two. 26 = 64 is too few; 27 = 128 is enough:

    n=[log⁡2100]=7that is, choose L = 128 = 2^(7)\begin{aligned} n &= [\log_{2} 100] = 7 \\ &\quad \text{that is, choose L = 128 = 2\textasciicircum} \\ &\quad \text{(7)} \end{aligned}n​=[log2​100]=7that is, choose L = 128 = 2^(7)​

    n = 7 bits/sample

  4. Aggregate bit rate for all 8 channels
    Total samplessec⁡=8×5⋅000=40⋅000\frac{\text{Total}\, \mathrm{samples}}{\sec} = 8 \times 5 \cdot 000 = 40 \cdot 000secTotalsamples​=8×5⋅000=40⋅000
    Rb=40⋅000×7=280⋅000 bits/sR_{b} = 40 \cdot 000 \times 7 = 280 \cdot 000\, \mathrm{bits/s}Rb​=40⋅000×7=280⋅000bits/s

    Rb = 280 kb/s

  5. Minimum bandwidth with raised-cosine pulses

    The raised-cosine bandwidth rule (proved in Module 3) is:

    BT=(Rb2)(1+α)=(280k2)×(1+0.2)=140k×1.2B_{T} = \left( \frac{R_{b}}{2} \right) (1 + \alpha) = \left( \frac{280 k}{2} \right) \times (1 + 0.2) = 140 k \times 1.2BT​=(2Rb​​)(1+α)=(2280k​)×(1+0.2)=140k×1.2

    BT = 168 kHz

Note on notation. Your PDF solves this twice, once using L and once using the symbol q for the number of levels, and writes the error rule as εmax = Δ/2 = mp/q ≤ 0.01 mp, where mp is the peak amplitude. Both routes give q ≥ 100 → q = 128 = 27 → 7 bits. Same answer, different letters. Do not let the change of symbol confuse you.

Exam tip — the standard PCM attack plan

Almost every PCM numerical is the same five moves in the same order. Write them down before you start:

  1. fs from fm  (watch for “25% above Nyquist” style twists)
  2. n from L, or L from an accuracy requirement, or n from Rb/fs
  3. Δ from Vpp/2n
  4. Rb = n fs  (multiply by N if it is TDM)
  5. SNR — either 6.02n + 1.76, or Vrms2/(Δ2/12)

Rounding rule: when n comes from a channel rate limit, round down (you cannot exceed the channel). When n comes from an accuracy requirement, round up (you must be at least that accurate).

03 From ninth.pdf and fifth.pdf — Tutorial 2

Line codes and baseband signalling

You have bits. Now you must turn them into actual voltages on a wire. The way you do that is called a line code, and the choice matters more than you would guess.

3.1 Data element versus signal element

Two words get used constantly from here on, and they are not the same thing. Your ninth.pdf opens with them, so we will too.

The two definitions

Data element — the smallest entity that can represent a piece of information. That is a bit.

Signal element — the shortest unit (timewise) of a digital signal.

Or, in the words of your slide: data elements are what we need to send; signal elements are what we can send practically, in a form the receiver can synchronise to, identify and interpret.

The link between them is a ratio called r: how many data elements ride on one signal element. It does not have to be 1.

In simple words

Think of signal elements as envelopes and data elements as letters.

r = 1 — one letter per envelope. Simple.
r = 2 — two letters stuffed in one envelope. Fewer envelopes needed, so less bandwidth — but the envelope must be able to show four different things (00, 01, 10, 11), so the levels sit closer together and noise hurts more.
r = ½ — one letter split across two envelopes. Wasteful of bandwidth, but the extra envelope gives you a guaranteed transition, which helps the receiver's clock. Manchester coding is exactly this.

Bigger r is more bandwidth-efficient. Smaller r is more robust. That trade-off runs through this whole module.

3.2 Data rate versus signal rate

Now put the two elements into per second form, and you get the two rates that students confuse most often.

Formula — the two rates and the link between them
Data rate N=number of data elements (bits) sent in 1sunit bps. Also called the bit rate.\begin{aligned} \text{Data rate}\, N &= \text{number of data elements}\, (\mathrm{bits})\, \text{sent in}\, 1 s \\ &\quad \text{unit bps. Also called the bit rate.} \end{aligned}Data rateN​=number of data elements(bits)sent in1sunit bps. Also called the bit rate.​

Signal rate S = number of signal elements sent in 1 s  —  unit baud. Also called the pulse rate, modulation rate or baud rate.

S = c × N × (1/r)   baud

S = signal rate  ·  c = the case factor  ·  N = data rate (bps)  ·  r = data elements per signal element

In simple words — what is that mysterious c?

The signal rate is not one fixed number, because it depends on the data pattern. Take NRZ-I: it only makes a transition when a 1 arrives. Send all zeros and the signal never changes — the worst case. Send alternating bits and it changes constantly — the best case.

So c is a fudge factor between 0 and 1 that says which case you are in. For an average, typical data stream we take c = ½. That is the value your slides use, and the value the exam expects unless it says otherwise.

Worked example — ninth.pdf, Example 1

Question. A signal is carrying data in which one data element is encoded as one signal element (r = 1). If the bit rate is 100 kbps, what is the average value of the baud rate if c is between 0 and 1?

  1. Take the average case factor

    c lies between 0 and 1, so the average value is

    c=12c = \frac{1}{2}c=21​
  2. Substitute into S = c × N × (1/r)
    S=12×100⋅000×(11)=50⋅000S = \frac{1}{2} \times 100 \cdot 000 \times \left( \frac{1}{1} \right) = 50 \cdot 000S=21​×100⋅000×(11​)=50⋅000

    S = 50 kbaud

Read the meaning: 100 000 bits per second travel using only 50 000 signal changes per second, on average. Baud and bps are not the same number, and here they differ by a factor of two purely because of the averaging.

Worked example — ninth.pdf, Example 2

Question. The maximum data rate of a channel is Nmax = 2 × B × log2 L (the Nyquist formula). Does this agree with the previous formula for Nmax?

  1. Work out how many bits one level carries

    A signal with L levels can carry log2 L bits per level. If each level corresponds to one signal element, then r = log2 L.

  2. Rearrange S = cN(1/r) for N, and use the average case c = ½

    The most signal elements a bandwidth B can carry is S = B, so

    Nmax⁡=(1c)×B×r=2×B×log⁡2LN_{\max} = \left( \frac{1}{c} \right) \times B \times r = 2 \times B \times \log_{2} LNmax​=(c1​)×B×r=2×B×log2​L

    Yes — the two formulas agree exactly

Why this matters. It shows that the general S = cN/r relationship and the famous Nyquist data-rate formula are the same statement wearing different clothes. The 1/c = 2 is where the “2” in 2B log2L comes from.

3.3 Why do we need line coding at all?

You could just put 0 V for a zero and 5 V for a one and be done. Your ninth.pdf spends four slides explaining why that naive choice breaks. Learn these four reasons — they are a standard exam question.

Reason 1 — Baseline wandering

In simple words

To decide whether an incoming voltage means 0 or 1, the receiver needs something to compare it against. So it keeps a running average of the received signal power. That average is called the baseline. Every incoming bit is judged against it.

Now send a long string of 1s. The running average creeps upward. Send a long string of 0s and it sags downward. This drift is called baseline wandering, and once the baseline has moved, the receiver starts judging bits against the wrong reference and makes mistakes.

A good line coding scheme must prevent baseline wandering.

Reason 2 — Lack of synchronization

If the receiver's clock does not tick at exactly the same rate as the sender's, it samples in the wrong places — and reads bits that were never sent.

Worked example — ninth.pdf, Example 3

Question. In a digital transmission, the receiver clock is 0.1 percent faster than the sender clock. How many extra bits per second does the receiver receive if the data rate is 1 kbps? How many if the data rate is 1 Mbps?

  1. At 1 kbps

    0.1% of 1000 is 1. So while 1000 bits are sent, the receiver clocks in 1001.

    1000 bits sent→1001 bits received1000\, \mathrm{bits}\, \text{sent} \to 1001\, \mathrm{bits}\, \text{received}1000bitssent→1001bitsreceived

    1 extra bit per second

  2. At 1 Mbps

    0.1% of 1 000 000 is 1000.

    1⋅000⋅000 bits sent→1⋅001⋅000 bits received1 \cdot 000 \cdot 000\, \mathrm{bits}\, \text{sent} \to 1 \cdot 001 \cdot 000\, \mathrm{bits}\, \text{received}1⋅000⋅000bitssent→1⋅001⋅000bitsreceived

    1000 extra bits per second

The lesson. The clock error is the same 0.1% in both cases, but the damage scales with speed. At 1 kbps you gain one junk bit a second; at 1 Mbps you gain a thousand. The faster you go, the more precisely the clocks must agree — which is exactly why high-speed links need self-synchronising line codes.

Reason 3 — DC components

In simple words

When the voltage in a digital signal stays constant for a while, Fourier analysis says the spectrum picks up very low frequencies. The frequencies right around zero are the DC (direct-current) components.

That is a problem, because many systems simply cannot pass low frequencies — particularly anything that uses transformer coupling, since a transformer only responds to changing current. Your slide gives the classic example: a telephone line cannot pass frequencies below 200 Hz. Any DC content you put into it is thrown away, and the signal arrives distorted.

So a good line code should have no DC component — its average voltage over time should be zero.

Reason 4 — Self-synchronization

In simple words

To interpret the signal correctly, the receiver's bit intervals must line up exactly with the sender's. If the receiver clock runs fast or slow, the intervals drift apart and bits get misread — as Example 3 just showed.

The fix is self-synchronization: build the timing information into the data itself. Your slide states the condition precisely — this works if there are transitions in the signal that alert the receiver to the beginning, middle or end of the pulse.

That single sentence is why Manchester coding exists. It guarantees a transition in the middle of every bit, so the receiver's clock is re-set every single bit period and can never drift.

Exam tip — the desirable properties of a line code

Tutorial 2 Example 3 asks exactly this. The answer is the four reasons above, turned into requirements:

  1. No DC component (so it survives transformers and telephone lines)
  2. No baseline wandering (so the decision threshold stays put)
  3. Self-synchronizing — plenty of transitions for clock recovery
  4. Small bandwidth (so it is cheap in spectrum)
  5. Built-in error detection (a bonus that AMI gives free)
  6. Immunity to noise, and low complexity/cost

3.4 The family tree of line codes

Your slide organises every scheme into five families. Learn this tree — it is a very common short-answer question.

The five families
FamilySchemesLevels used
UnipolarNRZ0 and +V (one polarity)
PolarNRZ (NRZ-L, NRZ-I), RZ, and biphase (Manchester, differential Manchester)−V and +V
BipolarAMI and pseudoternary−V, 0 and +V
Multilevel2B/1Q, 8B/6T, 4D-PAM5many
MultitransitionMLT-3three, but the transitions carry the meaning

3.5 The line codes you must be able to draw

These are the exact rules from your Tutorial 2 and your ninth.pdf. Learn them as rules first, then draw.

Line code rules
CodeLogic 1Logic 0
Unipolar NRZ+A for the full bit0 for the full bit
Unipolar RZ+A for half the bit, then back to 00 for the full bit
Polar NRZ-Lthe level says the bit: +A for one value, −A for the otherthe opposite level
Polar NRZ-Iinvert the level at the start of the bitdo not invert — hold the previous level
Polar RZ+A/2 for half the bit, then 0−A/2 for half the bit, then 0
Bipolar AMIalternates +A, −A, +A, −A …0 (no signal)
Pseudoternary0 (no signal)alternates +A, −A, +A …
Manchestertransition in the middle, low→hightransition in the middle, high→low
Differential Manchesterno transition at the start of the bittransition at the start of the bit — plus a mid-bit transition always
In simple words — decoding the names

NRZ = Non-Return to Zero. The voltage holds for the whole bit and does not come back to 0 in the middle.

RZ = Return to Zero. The voltage does its job for the first half of the bit, then returns to 0. This guarantees a transition in every 1-bit, which helps the clock — but the pulse is half as wide, so it needs twice the bandwidth.

Unipolar = one polarity (0 and +A). Polar = two polarities (−A and +A). Bipolar = three levels (−A, 0, +A).

AMI = Alternate Mark Inversion. “Mark” is old telegraph language for a 1. Every 1 flips the sign of the one before it: +A, −A, +A … Zeros are skipped in this counting. Pseudoternary is AMI with the roles of 0 and 1 swapped — nothing more.

Manchester — the rule is not about the level, it is about the direction of the jump in the middle. Every bit has a mid-bit transition, so the clock can never get lost.

Exam tip — “L” versus “I”, the difference that matters

NRZ-L is absolute; NRZ-I is differential.

In NRZ-L, the voltage level tells you the bit directly. Simple — but if the two wires get swapped somewhere in the cable, every single bit comes out inverted and the whole message is wrong.

In NRZ-I, the bit is carried by whether the level changed, not by the level itself. Swap the wires and the changes are still in the same places, so the data still decodes correctly. That immunity to polarity reversal is why differential schemes are used in practice.

Differential Manchester works the same way, and adds the guaranteed mid-bit transition on top — so it is both polarity-proof and self-clocking. That is why it was chosen for Token Ring.

3.6 Tutorial 2, Example 1 — drawing the waveforms

Question. Encode the data stream 1 1 0 0 0 0 1 0 into RZ, NRZ, AMI and Manchester codes.

Exam tip — how to draw these without mistakes
  1. Draw the vertical dashed lines for the bit boundaries first, and write the bits above them.
  2. For RZ codes, lightly mark the half-bit point too — that is where the pulse drops back to zero.
  3. For AMI, go through the bits and pencil + − + − above the 1s only, before you draw anything.
  4. For Manchester, remember it is about the middle jump direction, not the level. Some textbooks use the opposite convention, so always state which one you are using.

3.7 Bandwidth and power of each scheme

Your ninth.pdf gives each scheme a spectrum box with two numbers: the ratio r, and the average signal rate Save. Together with the power spectrum plot, they tell you what the scheme costs.

Worked example — ninth.pdf, Example 4

Question. A system is using NRZ-I to transfer data. What are the average signal rate and minimum bandwidth?

  1. Average signal rate

    For NRZ, the spectrum box gives

    Save=N2S_{\text{ave}} = \frac{N}{2}Save​=2N​
  2. Minimum bandwidth

    The minimum bandwidth needed equals the signal rate:

    Bmin⁡=SB_{\min} = SBmin​=S
  3. Put the numbers in (N = 1 Mbps)
    S=1⋅000⋅0002=500⋅000S = \frac{1 \cdot 000 \cdot 000}{2} = 500 \cdot 000S=21⋅000⋅000​=500⋅000

    S = 500 kbaud  ·  Bmin = 500 kHz

Correction — a slip in ninth.pdf, Example 4

The slide states the data rate as 10 Mbps but then prints the answer as 500 kbaud and 500 kHz. Those do not match: if N were really 10 Mbps, then N/2 would be 5 Mbaud and Bmin would be 5 MHz.

The printed answers correspond to N = 1 Mbps, which is the value in the original textbook this example comes from. So the method on the slide is right; only the stated data rate is a typo.

In the exam: use whatever N the question gives you, and apply S = N/2 then Bmin = S. If you are asked this exact question with 10 Mbps, the correct answers are 5 Mbaud and 5 MHz.

Comparing the spectra

In simple words — how to read that PSD plot

NRZ starts at its maximum at f = 0 and falls away. Big value at zero frequency = big DC component. Its first null is at fT = 1, so it is narrow — bandwidth-efficient but DC-heavy.

Bipolar (AMI) is zero at f = 0 and humps up around fT ≈ 0.5. Zero at DC is exactly what we wanted, and its bandwidth is no worse than NRZ. This is the best of both, which is why AMI was the workhorse of telephone trunk lines.

Manchester is also zero at DC but its hump sits further out, near fT ≈ 0.75, and stretches wider. So Manchester buys perfect clock recovery and no DC at the price of roughly double the bandwidth.

Line code comparison — the summary to memorise
SchemerSaveDC?Self-clocking?Bandwidth
Unipolar NRZ1N/2Yes, worstNoNarrow
Polar NRZ-L / NRZ-I1N/2YesNoNarrow
Polar RZ½NNoYesDouble
Bipolar AMI1N/2NoOnly on 1sNarrow
Manchester½NNoYes, alwaysDouble
Diff. Manchester½NNoYes, alwaysDouble
Exam tip — AMI's free error detection, and its one weakness

Because AMI's 1s must strictly alternate +A, −A, +A, −A, the receiver can spot an error for free: if two consecutive 1s have the same sign, something went wrong. This is called a bipolar violation. No extra bits were spent to get it.

But AMI has one weakness. Zeros are sent as nothing at all, so a long run of zeros means a long silence — and the receiver's clock drifts. That is precisely the problem scrambling (section 3.8) was invented to solve.

3.8 Bit rate versus pulse rate, revisited

Section 3.2 gave the general relationship. Tutorial 2 asks you to apply it to two waveforms, so let us do it.

Formula — bit rate from pulse rate

Pulse rate = 1 / (duration of one pulse)   pulses/sec, also called baud

Bit rate = Pulse rate × log2 L   bits/sec

L = number of different voltage levels the pulse can take

In simple words

A pulse (or symbol, or signal element) is one blob of signal. The pulse rate counts how many blobs go past per second.

How many bits does one blob carry? That depends on how many different shapes a blob can have. Two levels → 1 bit (log2 2 = 1). Four levels → 2 bits. Sixteen levels → 4 bits.

So bit rate is always ≥ pulse rate. They are equal only for binary signalling. This is exactly why modern systems use 256-QAM: one symbol carries 8 bits instead of 1.

Worked example — Tutorial 2, Example 2

Question. For the signals shown in figures 13.5(a) and (b), determine the bit rate and pulse rate. The bit duration Tb = 0.5 ms.

Figure (a) — two levels (0 or A), one pulse lasts exactly one bit.

  1. Pulse rate
    Pulse rate=1Tb=10.5×10−3\text{Pulse rate} = \frac{1}{T_{b}} = \frac{1}{0.5 \times 10^{- 3}}Pulse rate=Tb​1​=0.5×10−31​

    2000 pulses/sec

  2. Bit rate

    Two levels, so L = 2 and log2 2 = 1:

    Bit rate=2000×1\text{Bit rate} = 2000 \times 1Bit rate=2000×1

    2000 bps

Figure (b) — multilevel (−A, −A/2, 0, +A/2, +A), one pulse lasts two bit periods.

  1. Pulse duration and pulse rate
    pulse duration=2Tb=1 ms\text{pulse duration} = 2 T_{b} = 1\, \mathrm{ms}pulse duration=2Tb​=1ms
    Pulse rate=11×10−3\text{Pulse rate} = \frac{1}{1 \times 10^{- 3}}Pulse rate=1×10−31​

    1000 pulses/sec

  2. Bit rate

    Here L = 4, so log2 4 = 2:

    Bit rate=1000×2\text{Bit rate} = 1000 \times 2Bit rate=1000×2

    2000 bps

The lesson. Both signals carry the same 2000 bits per second. But (b) does it with half as many pulses per second, by making each pulse carry 2 bits instead of 1. Half the pulse rate means roughly half the bandwidth. That is the whole idea behind multilevel signalling — and the price is that the levels sit closer together, so noise flips them more easily.

3.9 Scrambling

Section 3.7 left AMI with one unsolved problem: a long run of zeros means a long silence, and the clock drifts. Your ninth.pdf gives the fix.

The problem and the idea

Your slide states it in three lines:

  • A long sequence of 0s upsets the synchronization.
  • If we can find a way to avoid a long sequence of 0s in the original stream, we can use bipolar AMI and others for long distances.
  • One solution is called scrambling.

Scrambling shuffles the data into a random-looking stream that has no long runs of zeros — without adding a single extra bit. That last part is what makes it different from line coding and from channel coding.

Formula — scrambler and descrambler equations

Scrambler:   S ⊕ D3T ⊕ D5T = T

Rearranged:   S = T ⊕ (D3 ⊕ D5)T = [1 ⊕ (D3 ⊕ D5)]T = (1 ⊕ F)T

Descrambler:   T ⊕ FT = T ⊕ (D3 ⊕ D5)T = S

S = input data · T = scrambled output · ⊕ = XOR · Dn = “delayed by n bits” · F = D3 ⊕ D5

In simple words

Dn just means “the same stream, but n bits late”. So D3T is the transmitted stream delayed by 3 bits — which is exactly what tapping stage 3 of the shift register gives you.

The scrambler XORs the incoming data with two delayed copies of its own output. That feedback is what makes the result look random.

And the beauty of XOR is that it undoes itself: x ⊕ y ⊕ y = x. So running the identical circuit at the far end recovers S exactly. No key, no extra bits, no negotiation.

Worked example — ninth.pdf, Example 7.2

Question. The data stream 101010100000111 is fed to the scrambler. Find the scrambler output T, assuming the initial contents of the registers are zero.

  1. Follow the feedback round and round

    Initially T = S. That S enters the register and comes back as (D3 ⊕ D5)S = FS. That new sequence enters again and returns as F2S, and so on. So

    T = S ⊕ FS ⊕ F2S ⊕ F3S ⊕ …

      = (1 ⊕ F ⊕ F2 ⊕ F3 ⊕ …) S

  2. Work out F2, using the XOR cancellation trick

    F2 = (D3 ⊕ D5)(D3 ⊕ D5) = D6 ⊕ D10 ⊕ D8 ⊕ D8

    Modulo-2 addition of any sequence with itself is zero, so D8 ⊕ D8 = 0:

    F2 = D6 ⊕ D10

  3. And F3

    F3 = (D6 ⊕ D10)(D3 ⊕ D5) = D9 ⊕ D11 ⊕ D13 ⊕ D15

  4. Collect all the delay terms

    T = (1 ⊕ D3 ⊕ D5 ⊕ D6 ⊕ D9 ⊕ D10 ⊕ D11 ⊕ D12 ⊕ D13 ⊕ D15 …) S

  5. Write out each delayed copy and XOR the columns

    Because DnS is simply S shifted right by n places:

    S101010100000111
    D3S000101010100000111
    D5S00000101010100000111
    D6S000000101010100000111
    D9S000000000101010100000111
    D10S0000000000101010100000111
    D11S00000000000101010100000111
    D12S000000000000101010100000111
    D13S0000000000000101010100000111
    D15S000000000000000101010100000111
    T101110001101001

    T = 101110001101001

Did it work? Look at the two streams. The input 101010100000111 contains a run of five zeros. The output 101110001101001 has a longest run of only three. The clock now gets a transition often enough to stay locked — and not one extra bit was transmitted.

3.10 How data is actually sent: transmission modes

Your ninth.pdf closes this part with the practical question of how bits leave the machine.

The transmission modes tree
ModeSub-modeWhat it means
Parallel—All bits of a group travel at once, on separate wires.
SerialAsynchronousEach character framed with start and stop bits; gaps allowed between characters.
SynchronousContinuous stream of frames, no gaps, no start/stop bits.
IsochronousFixed, guaranteed timing between frames — needed for live audio and video.
In simple words — why serial won

Parallel looks eight times faster, and over a few centimetres it is. But over any real distance it fails, for two reasons.

Cost: eight wires cost eight times as much as one.

Skew: no two wires are exactly the same length or have exactly the same delay. Over a long cable the eight bits that left together arrive at slightly different times, and the further and faster you go the worse it gets. A single wire has nothing to skew against.

That is why old parallel printer ports and IDE ribbon cables were replaced by USB, SATA and PCIe — all serial. Parallel survives only inside a chip or across a circuit board, where distances are tiny.

Exam tip — asynchronous vs synchronous in one line each

Asynchronous: cheap, simple, forgiving of clock error, but wastes 2 bits of overhead on every 8 bits of data (20% loss). Used for keyboards, old modems, simple serial ports.

Synchronous: no per-character overhead so much faster, but needs proper clock recovery. Used for everything high-speed.

Isochronous: synchronous plus a guarantee about timing — frames arrive at a fixed rate with bounded delay. Needed for real-time audio and video, where arriving late is as bad as not arriving.

04 From ninth.pdf — Syllabus Unit 2

Bandlimited channels, ISI and equalization

This is Unit 2 of your syllabus, in full. Every channel has limited bandwidth, and that single fact causes one specific disease — intersymbol interference. This module is the diagnosis, the prevention, and the cure.

4.1 What goes wrong on a bandlimited channel

Module 3 gave you neat rectangular pulses. Real channels do not pass rectangles. A rectangle contains frequencies stretching out to infinity, and a channel with bandwidth B chops all of them off above B. What comes out the far end is a smeared, spread-out version of what went in.

In simple words — what ISI is

ISI = Intersymbol Interference. The tail of pulse number 1 is still hanging around when pulse number 2 is being read, so they add together and the receiver decides the wrong value.

Picture shouting a word in a large empty hall. The echo of your first word is still bouncing around when you say the second, and the listener hears a muddle. ISI is exactly that, in electrical form.

And notice something important from the figure: ISI is not noise. No random hiss was added. The signal interfered with itself, purely because the channel was too narrow. You cannot fix it by shouting louder.

The second source of ISI: multipath

In a wireless channel there is a second, quite different cause of the same disease.

In simple words

Your signal takes several routes to the receiver at once — one straight, others bouncing off buildings. The bounced copies travel further, so they arrive late. A late copy of symbol 1 lands on top of symbol 2. That is ISI again, arriving by a different door.

This is why ISI is the central problem of mobile communication, and why the whole of OFDM (Unit 5 of your syllabus) exists to defeat it.

4.2 The ISI equation

Now the mathematics. Your slide splits the received signal into exactly the pieces we care about.

Formula — the received signal, split into three parts
y(t)=μ∑kakp(t−kTb)+n(t)y(t) = \mu \sum_{k} a_{k} p(t - kT_{b}) + n(t)y(t)=μk∑​ak​p(t−kTb​)+n(t)

Sampling at the i-th instant ti:

y(ti)=μai+μ∑k≠iakp[(i−k)Tb]+n(ti)y(t_{i}) = \mu a_{i} + \mu \sum_{k \ne i} a_{k} p [(i - k) T_{b}] + n(t_{i})y(ti​)=μai​+μk=i∑​ak​p[(i−k)Tb​]+n(ti​)

ak = the k-th transmitted bit · p(t) = the pulse shape · Tb = bit period · μ = a scale factor · n(t) = noise

In simple words — read the three terms

Term 1, μai — the contribution of the bit you actually wanted. This is the signal.

Term 2, the sum with k ≠ i — the ISI. Your slide calls it “the residual effect of all other transmitted bits”. Every other bit contributes a little bit of its tail at this sampling instant. Note the condition k ≠ i: we deliberately exclude the wanted bit and sum up everyone else.

Term 3, n(ti) — the noise.

So the receiver's job is to read term 1 while terms 2 and 3 try to fool it. And here is the design goal: we want to make term 2 exactly zero. That is what the rest of this module achieves.

Exam tip — a line worth quoting

Your slide ends with a sentence examiners love:

“When the signal-to-noise ratio is high, as is the case in a telephone system, the operation of the system is largely limited by ISI rather than noise.”

In other words: on a good, quiet wire, noise is not your enemy — your own pulse tails are. Turning up the power does not help at all, because the ISI grows in exactly the same proportion as the signal.

4.3 Nyquist's three criteria

Harry Nyquist asked the key question: the pulses are going to spread and overlap no matter what — so can we still read them correctly? His answer is the foundation of this whole subject.

Nyquist's insight, from your slide

“Pulse amplitudes can be detected correctly despite pulse spreading or overlapping, if there is no ISI at the decision-making instants.”

Read that carefully, because it is cleverer than it first looks. Nyquist does not say “stop the pulses overlapping”. He accepts that they will overlap. He only insists that at the exact instants when the receiver looks, the interference happens to be zero.

Think of a room full of people talking. You do not need silence — you only need everyone else to happen to pause at the exact moment your friend says each word.

The three criteria
CriterionConditionWhat it protects
1stAt sampling points, no ISIThe pulse centres — so the amplitude you read is correct
2ndAt threshold, no ISIThe pulse edges (zero crossings) — so timing recovery works
3rdAreas within the symbol period are zero, then no ISIThe area under the pulse — used by integrating receivers

4.4 The first Nyquist criterion — time domain

Formula — the first Nyquist criterion in time
Let 1T be the sample rate⋅The pulse p(t) must satisfy\frac{\text{Let}\, 1}{T}\, \text{be the sample rate} \cdot \text{The pulse}\, p(t)\, \text{must satisfy}TLet1​be the sample rate⋅The pulsep(t)must satisfy
p(nT)=1whenn=0p(nT) = 1 \quad\text{when}\quad n = 0p(nT)=1whenn=0
p(nT)=0whenn≠0p(nT) = 0 \quad\text{when}\quad n \ne 0p(nT)=0whenn=0
In simple words

The pulse must be tall (value 1) at its own sampling instant, and exactly zero at every other sampling instant. Between those instants it can do whatever it likes — wander, ring, overshoot. Nobody is looking then.

4.5 The first Nyquist criterion — frequency domain

The time-domain condition is easy to state but hard to check. Nyquist's real contribution was showing it has an exactly equivalent form in frequency, which is easy to check.

Formula — the first Nyquist criterion in frequency

The necessary and sufficient condition for p(nT) = 1, 0, 0, 0 … is that its Fourier transform P(f) satisfies

∑m=−∞∞P(f+mT)=T\sum_{m = - \infty}^{\infty} P\left( f + \frac{m}{T} \right) = Tm=−∞∑∞​P(f+Tm​)=T
In simple words — the folding test

This looks frightening. It is actually a recipe you could do with scissors:

  1. Draw the pulse's spectrum P(f).
  2. Make copies of it, shifted left and right by the symbol rate 1/T, 2/T, and so on.
  3. Stack all the copies on top of each other and add them up.
  4. If the total comes out as a flat horizontal line (a constant, T), the pulse has zero ISI. If the total is bumpy, it does not.

The shifted copies must overlap in exactly such a way that wherever one is falling, the neighbour is rising by the same amount — so the sum stays level. That property is called having odd symmetry about the band edge, and it is the whole secret.

4.6 Sample rate versus bandwidth — the three cases

Now the practical question: given a channel of bandwidth W, how fast can I signal? Your slide gives three cases, and the answer is different in each.

The three cases, where W is the bandwidth of P(f)
CaseWhat happens
1/T > 2WNo function can satisfy the Nyquist condition. Zero-ISI signalling is impossible.
1/T = 2WExactly one solution: the rectangular spectrum (a sinc pulse in time). The minimum-bandwidth case.
1/T < 2WMany solutions exist. “A typical one is the raised cosine function.”
Formula — the 1/T = 2W solution
p(t)=sin⁡(πtT)πt=sinc⁡(πtT)p(t) = \frac{\sin\left( \frac{\pi t}{T} \right)}{\pi t} = \operatorname{sinc}\left( \frac{\pi t}{T} \right)p(t)=πtsin(Tπt​)​=sinc(Tπt​)

P(f) = T for |f| < W,   0 otherwise   (a perfect rectangle)

In simple words — why the perfect case is useless

Case 2 sounds ideal: minimum possible bandwidth, exactly one right answer. But the sinc pulse has two fatal practical problems.

It needs a brick-wall filter. A spectrum that is flat up to W and then drops instantly to zero cannot be built with real components. Real filters roll off gradually.

Its tails die away far too slowly. The sinc decays only as 1/t, so a pulse from twenty symbols ago is still contributing. If your sampling clock is off by even a hair, all those slowly-dying tails no longer cancel, and the ISI is catastrophic.

So we accept case 3 — use a bit more bandwidth than the theoretical minimum, in exchange for a filter that can actually be built and tails that die quickly. That compromise pulse is the raised cosine.

4.7 The raised cosine filter

Formula — the raised cosine pulse

Time domain (a sinc multiplied by a cosine correction):

prc(t)=[sin⁡(πtT)πtT]×[cos⁡(rπtT)1−(2rtT)2]p_{rc}(t) = \left[ \frac{\sin\left( \frac{\pi t}{T} \right)}{\frac{\pi t}{T}} \right] \times \left[ \frac{\cos\left( \frac{r \pi t}{T} \right)}{1 - \left( \frac{2 rt}{T} \right)^{2}} \right]prc​(t)=[Tπt​sin(Tπt​)​]×[1−(T2rt​)2cos(Trπt​)​]

Frequency domain, with r the roll-off factor, 0 ≤ r ≤ 1:

P(f)=1forf≤1−r2TP(f) = 1 \quad\text{for}\quad f \le \frac{1 - r}{2 T}P(f)=1forf≤2T1−r​
P(f)=12[1+cos⁡((π2r)(πfT+r−1))]for(1−r)2T≤f≤1+r2TP(f) = \frac{\frac{1}{2 \left[ 1 + \cos\left( \left( \frac{\pi}{2 r} \right) \left( \frac{\pi f}{T} + r - 1 \right) \right) \right]} \quad\text{for}\quad (1 - r)}{2 T} \le f \le \frac{1 + r}{2 T}P(f)=2T2[1+cos((2rπ​)(Tπf​+r−1))]1​for(1−r)​≤f≤2T1+r​
P(f)=0forf≥1+r2TP(f) = 0 \quad\text{for}\quad f \ge \frac{1 + r}{2 T}P(f)=0forf≥2T1+r​
In simple words

Do not be scared by the three-part definition. It is just describing a shape with three regions: flat on top, a smooth cosine-shaped slope down the sides, then zero. That is literally why it is called a “raised cosine” — a cosine curve lifted up so it sits above zero.

The time-domain formula is the sinc pulse from case 2, multiplied by an extra factor that squashes the tails down quickly. You keep the zero-crossings that give you zero ISI, but you lose the slowly-dying tails that made the sinc so fragile.

Note on symbols: your ninth.pdf writes the roll-off factor as r. Your Tutorial 2 writes the same thing as α. They are identical — do not let the change of letter confuse you.

Formula — raised cosine bandwidth (the exam version)
fB=1+α2Tbf_{B} = \frac{1 + \alpha}{2 T_{b}}fB​=2Tb​1+α​

Equivalently, since Rb = 1/Tb:    BT = (Rb/2)(1 + α)

In simple words

Rb/2 is the absolute theoretical minimum — the Nyquist bandwidth. You can never do better.

The factor (1 + α) is the penalty you pay above that minimum:

  • α = 0 → bandwidth = Rb/2. The ideal brick wall. Impossible to build, fragile.
  • α = 1 → bandwidth = Rb. Double the minimum. Wasteful, but very forgiving.
  • α = 0.2 to 0.5 → the practical compromise everybody actually uses.
Worked example — Tutorial 2, Example 4

Question. A communication channel of bandwidth 75 kHz is required to transmit binary data at a rate of 0.1 Mb/s using raised-cosine pulses. Determine the roll-off factor α.

  1. Find the bit duration
    Tb=1Rb=10.1×106=10−5sT_{b} = \frac{1}{R_{b}} = \frac{1}{0.1 \times 10^{6}} = 10^{- 5} sTb​=Rb​1​=0.1×1061​=10−5s
  2. Write down the given bandwidth
    fB=75 kHz=75×103Hzf_{B} = 75\, \mathrm{kHz} = 75 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{Hz}fB​=75kHz=75×103Hz
  3. Rearrange for (1 + α)

    From fB = (1+α)/(2Tb), multiply both sides by 2Tb:

    1+α=2fBTb=2×(75×103)×10−5=1.51 + \alpha = 2 f_{B} T_{b} = 2 \times (75 \times 10^{3}) \times 10^{- 5} = 1.51+α=2fB​Tb​=2×(75×103)×10−5=1.5
  4. Solve for α
    α=1.5−1\alpha = 1.5 - 1α=1.5−1

    α = 0.5

Sanity check. The Nyquist minimum for 0.1 Mb/s would be 50 kHz. We were given 75 kHz, which is 1.5 times the minimum — so α = 0.5. The answer agrees with common sense.

Exam tip — and don't forget Tutorial 2 Example 5

The three raised-cosine question types are all the same equation rearranged:

  • Given Rb and α → find BT. (Tutorial 2 Example 5, solved in Module 2)
  • Given Rb and BT → find α. (Example 4 above)
  • Given BT and α → find the maximum Rb.

The full telemetry problem — eight TDM channels, 1% accuracy, α = 0.2, answer 168 kHz — is worked step by step in Module 2, section 2.7. It chains sampling, quantization, TDM and this bandwidth formula into one question, so it is the single best revision problem in your materials.

4.8 Bandwidth efficiency

Now we can answer the practical question: how many bits per second do I get per hertz of spectrum?

Formula — transmission (bandwidth) efficiency
βrc=data ratebandwidth=1T[1+r2T]=21+rbit/s per Hz\begin{aligned} \beta_{rc} &= \frac{\text{data rate}}{\text{bandwidth}} = \frac{\frac{1}{T}}{\left[ \frac{1 + r}{2 T} \right]} = \frac{2}{1 + r} && \text{bit/s per Hz} \end{aligned}βrc​​=bandwidthdata rate​=[2T1+r​]T1​​=1+r2​​​bit/s per Hz​

Rearranged for design:

Rb=2Bt1+randBt=Rb(1+r)2R_{b} = \frac{2 B_{t}}{1 + r} \quad\text{and}\quad B_{t} = \frac{R_{b}(1 + r)}{2}Rb​=1+r2Bt​​andBt​=2Rb​(1+r)​

Range:   1 bit/s/Hz ≤ 2/(1+r) < 2 bit/s/Hz

In simple words — the two ends of the range

r = 0 gives 2/(1+0) = 2 bits/s/Hz. The theoretical best for binary signalling. Requires the impossible brick-wall filter.

r = 1 gives 2/(1+1) = 1 bit/s/Hz. The worst efficiency, but the easiest filter to build — and, as your slide notes, this is the case that also satisfies the 2nd Nyquist criterion.

So the whole design space for a raised-cosine system lives between 1 and 2 bits per second per hertz, and choosing r is choosing where on that line you sit.

4.9 The second Nyquist criterion

The first criterion protected the pulse centres. The second protects the pulse edges.

Formula — the second Nyquist criterion

Values at the pulse edge are distortionless:

p(t) = 0.5 when t = −T/2 or T/2

p(t)=0whent=(2k−1)T2,fork≠0,1p(t) = 0 \quad\text{when}\quad t = \frac{(2 k - 1) T}{2}, \quad\text{for}\quad k \ne 0, 1p(t)=0whent=2(2k−1)T​,fork=0,1

In frequency, over −1/T ≤ f ≤ 1/T:

Pr(f)=Re[∑n(−1)nP(f+nT)]=Tcos⁡(fT2)P_{r}(f) = Re \left[ \sum_{n} (- 1)^{n} P\left( f + \frac{n}{T} \right) \right] = T \cos\left( \frac{fT}{2} \right)Pr​(f)=Re[n∑​(−1)nP(f+Tn​)]=Tcos(2fT​)
Pi(f)=Im[∑n(−1)nP(f+nT)]=0P_{i}(f) = Im \left[ \sum_{n} (- 1)^{n} P\left( f + \frac{n}{T} \right) \right] = 0Pi​(f)=Im[n∑​(−1)nP(f+Tn​)]=0
In simple words — why anyone cares about the edges

The receiver does not only need to know what the value is — it needs to know when to look. It works out the timing from the zero crossings of the received waveform, because those are the sharpest, most identifiable features.

If ISI moves those crossings around, the recovered clock jitters, and a jittery clock samples in the wrong place — which undoes all the work the first criterion did.

So: 1st criterion → correct amplitudes. 2nd criterion → correct timing. A system that satisfies both is clean in value and in time.

4.10 The eye diagram

Everything above is theory. The eye diagram is how an engineer sees ISI on an oscilloscope in about two seconds.

In simple words — how an eye diagram is made

Take the received waveform. Chop it into pieces exactly one symbol period long. Now lay every piece on top of every other piece, all starting at the same point.

If the channel is clean, every piece follows nearly the same path, so the overlaid picture has a big empty gap in the middle — it looks like an eye. If there is ISI, the pieces take many different paths, the traces spread out, and the eye closes.

On a real oscilloscope you do not chop anything: you just trigger the scope at the symbol rate and let the traces pile up by themselves.

The six labels on an eye diagram — learn all of them
Optimum sampling instantat the point of maximum eye opening. Samplehere.\begin{aligned} \text{Optimum sampling instant} & \\ &\quad \text{at the point of maximum eye opening. Sample} \\ &\quad \text{here.} \end{aligned}Optimum sampling instant​at the point of maximum eye opening. Samplehere.​
Noise marginthe vertical opening at the best samplingpoint. How much noise you can take before anerror.\begin{aligned} \text{Noise margin} & \\ &\quad \text{the vertical opening at the best sampling} \\ &\quad \text{point. How much noise you can take before an} \\ &\quad \text{error.} \end{aligned}Noise margin​the vertical opening at the best samplingpoint. How much noise you can take before anerror.​
Slopeshows sensitivity to sampling time. Steepsides mean a small timing error hurts a lot.\begin{aligned} \text{Slope} & \\ &\quad \text{shows sensitivity to sampling time. Steep} \\ &\quad \text{sides mean a small timing error hurts a lot.} \end{aligned}Slope​shows sensitivity to sampling time. Steepsides mean a small timing error hurts a lot.​
Level−crossing ambiguitythe spread of the zero crossings. This is thetiming jitter.\begin{aligned} \text{Level} - \text{crossing ambiguity} & \\ &\quad \text{the spread of the zero crossings. This is the} \\ &\quad \text{timing jitter.} \end{aligned}Level−crossing ambiguity​the spread of the zero crossings. This is thetiming jitter.​
Distortion at the best sampling pointhow much the trace has thickened, i.e. theISI.\begin{aligned} \text{Distortion at the best sampling point} & \\ &\quad \text{how much the trace has thickened, i.e. the} \\ &\quad \text{ISI.} \end{aligned}Distortion at the best sampling point​how much the trace has thickened, i.e. theISI.​
Error−free sampling regionthe horizontal width of the eye. How muchtiming error you can tolerate.\begin{aligned} \text{Error} - \text{free sampling region} & \\ &\quad \text{the horizontal width of the eye. How much} \\ &\quad \text{timing error you can tolerate.} \end{aligned}Error−free sampling region​the horizontal width of the eye. How muchtiming error you can tolerate.​
In simple words — the one sentence to remember

A wide-open eye means a healthy link. A closing eye means trouble — vertically it is losing noise margin, horizontally it is losing timing margin.

An eye that has closed completely means the ISI alone is enough to cause errors, with no noise required at all.

Reading the eye pattern figure — what each roll-off gives you
r1st Nyquist2nd Nyquistth/TWhat the eye looks like
1YesYes1.00Wide open and clean
0.8YesNo0.93Still very good
0.5YesNo0.80More cluttered, overshoot to ±1.5
→ 0YesNo0.32Nearly closed, overshoot to ±3
In simple words — what th/T is telling you

th/T is the fraction of the symbol period in which you can safely sample. It is the horizontal width of the eye, as a fraction of one symbol.

At r = 1 it is 1.00 — you could sample anywhere in the symbol and still be right. At r → 0 it collapses to 0.32 — you must hit a window less than a third of a symbol wide, or you make errors.

And look at the overshoot column: at r → 0 the waveform swings to ±3 instead of ±1. That means your amplifier must handle three times the voltage, so it costs power as well as timing accuracy.

So the “free” bandwidth saving of a small roll-off is not free at all. You pay for it in timing precision and in transmitter power. That is why practical systems sit around r = 0.2 to 0.5.

4.11 How the pulse is actually generated

We have decided what shape we want. How does a circuit build it?

In simple words

A transversal filter is just a row of delay boxes with a multiplier hanging off each one, all feeding an adder. Nothing more.

The clever part is the choice of multipliers: the tap weights are the samples of the pulse you want to build. So if you want a raised cosine, you sample a raised cosine, store those numbers as the coefficients, and the circuit reproduces the shape every time an input pulse arrives.

Remember this structure — the zero-forcing equalizer in section 4.13 is the exact same circuit, used backwards.

4.12 Regenerative repeaters

Signals fade over distance. Before we can talk about fixing ISI, we need to talk about what sits along the route.

Formula — channel attenuation
r(t)=αs(t)+n(t),0≤α≤1r(t) = \alpha s(t) + n(t), 0 \le \alpha \le 1r(t)=αs(t)+n(t),0≤α≤1
If the transmitted energy is Eb,the received energy is α2Eb,so the received SNRisα2EbN0If\, \text{the transmitted energy is}\, E_{b}, \text{the received energy is}\, \alpha^{2} E_{b}, \frac{\text{so the received}\, \mathrm{SNR} \quad\text{is}\quad \alpha^{2} E_{b}}{N_{0}}Ifthe transmitted energy isEb​,the received energy isα2Eb​,N0​so the receivedSNRisα2Eb​​
In simple words

α is the fraction of your signal that survives the journey. Since power goes as voltage squared, an α of 0.1 means you keep only 0.01 — one percent — of your power.

Meanwhile the noise n(t) is added after the attenuation, at full strength. So the signal shrinks and the noise does not, and your SNR collapses. As your slide puts it: this makes the system more vulnerable to the additive noise.

Analog repeater

An amplifier. It boosts the signal strength along the path.

But it boosts the noise too — your slide calls this noise propagation. Every hop adds a little more noise on top of the noise already there, and it accumulates forever. After twenty hops the signal is unusable.

Regenerative repeater

It detects and regenerates a clean, noise-free signal.

It decides “that was a 1”, throws the noisy waveform away, and builds a brand new perfect 1. The noise does not accumulate at all. Used on wire line, fibre and wireless systems.

In simple words — the one big advantage, and the one catch

The advantage: this is the deepest reason digital beats analog. An analog chain accumulates noise at every hop and can never recover. A digital chain resets to perfect at every repeater. You can cross an ocean with no degradation at all.

The catch, stated on your slide: “if an error occurs in the detector, this error is propagated forward.” Once a repeater decides wrongly, it regenerates that wrong bit perfectly, and every repeater after it faithfully passes on the mistake. Nothing downstream can tell it was ever wrong.

The three functions of a regenerative repeater — memorise these

1. Reshaping incoming pulses by means of an equalizer.

2. Extracting the timing information required to sample incoming pulses at optimum instants.

3. Making symbol detection decisions based on the pulse samples.

4.13 The zero-forcing equalizer

Function 1 of the repeater was “reshaping by means of an equalizer”. This is that equalizer.

In simple words — the idea in one line

The channel smeared the pulse. An equalizer is a filter that applies the opposite smear, so the two cancel and a clean pulse comes out.

Physically it is the same tapped-delay-line from section 4.11, but now the tap weights are chosen to undo the channel rather than to build a pulse.

Formula — the equalizer output and the design condition

Output at the k-th sampling instant:

po[k]=∑n=−NNcnpr[k−n]k=0,±1,±2,…p_{o} [k] = \sum_{n = - N}^{N} c_{n} p_{r} [k - n] k = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dotspo​[k]=n=−N∑N​cn​pr​[k−n]k=0,±1,±2,…

The first Nyquist criterion demands:

po[k]=1fork=0,po[k]=0fork=±1,±2,…,±Np_{o} [k] = 1 \quad\text{for}\quad k = 0, p_{o} [k] = 0 \quad\text{for}\quad k = \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots, \pm Npo​[k]=1fork=0,po​[k]=0fork=±1,±2,…,±N
In simple words — and where the name comes from

Your slide is refreshingly honest about the limitation. Substituting the Nyquist condition gives an infinite set of simultaneous equations in only 2N+1 unknowns. You cannot possibly solve them all.

So we compromise: we force the 2N nearest neighbours to zero and simply accept whatever happens further out. That is literally where the name comes from — you are forcing zeros at the sampling instants you can reach.

A 3-tap equalizer kills the ISI from the one symbol either side. A 5-tap kills two either side. More taps means better cancellation and more cost.

Formula — the matrix equation to solve
Po=Prc→c=Pr−1PoP_{o} = P_{r} c \to c = P_{r}^{- 1} P_{o}Po​=Pr​c→c=Pr−1​Po​

Po = target vector [0 … 0 1 0 … 0]T with the 1 in the middle

Pr = matrix of received-pulse samples, each row shifted one place from the last

c = the tap weights [c−N … c0 … cN]T you are solving for

Worked example — ninth.pdf, Example 7.3 (design a 3-tap equalizer)

Question. For the received pulse pr(t), let

pr[0]=1p_{r} [0] = 1pr​[0]=1
pr[1]=−0.3pr[2]=0.1p_{r} [1] = - 0.3 p_{r} [2] = 0.1pr​[1]=−0.3pr​[2]=0.1
pr[−1]=−0.2pr[−2]=0.05p_{r} [- 1] = - 0.2 p_{r} [- 2] = 0.05pr​[−1]=−0.2pr​[−2]=0.05

Design a three-tap (N = 1) equalizer.

  1. Understand what you have been given

    The received pulse should have been 1 at its own instant and 0 everywhere else. Instead it is −0.3 one symbol later, −0.2 one symbol earlier, and so on. Those non-zero values are the ISI we must cancel.

  2. Set up the matrix

    N = 1 means three taps: c−1, c0, c1. Each row of the matrix shifts the index by one:

    row 1 uses pr[0],pr[−1],pr[−2]\text{row}\, 1\, \text{uses}\, p_{r} [0], p_{r} [- 1], p_{r} [- 2]row1usespr​[0],pr​[−1],pr​[−2]
    row 2 uses pr[1],pr[0],pr[−1]\text{row}\, 2\, \text{uses}\, p_{r} [1], p_{r} [0], p_{r} [- 1]row2usespr​[1],pr​[0],pr​[−1]
    row 3 uses pr[2],pr[1],pr[0]\text{row}\, 3\, \text{uses}\, p_{r} [2], p_{r} [1], p_{r} [0]row3usespr​[2],pr​[1],pr​[0]
  3. Write it out

    ┌ 0 ┐    ┌  1   −0.2   0.05 ┐ ┌ c−1 ┐

    │ 1 │ = │ −0.3   1   −0.2  │ │ c0  │

    └ 0 ┘    └  0.1  −0.3   1    ┘ └ c1  ┘

    The left-hand vector is the target: we want the output to be 0 one symbol early, 1 at the centre, and 0 one symbol late.

  4. Solve the three simultaneous equations
    c−1−0.2c0+0.05c1=0c_{- 1} - 0.2 c_{0} + 0.05 c_{1} = 0c−1​−0.2c0​+0.05c1​=0
    −0.3c−1+c0−0.2c1=1- 0.3 c_{- 1} + c_{0} - 0.2 c_{1} = 1−0.3c−1​+c0​−0.2c1​=1
    0.1c−1−0.3c0+c1=00.1 c_{- 1} - 0.3 c_{0} + c_{1} = 00.1c−1​−0.3c0​+c1​=0

    c−1 = 0.210  ·  c0 = 1.13  ·  c1 = 0.318

  5. Confirm what that buys you

    As your slide states, this tap setting assures that

    po[0]=1andpo[−1]=po[1]=0p_{o} [0] = 1 \quad\text{and}\quad p_{o} [- 1] = p_{o} [1] = 0po​[0]=1andpo​[−1]=po​[1]=0

    The ISI from the symbol either side has been cancelled exactly.

Read the answer. The centre tap c0 = 1.13 is the biggest, which makes sense — most of the output is the pulse itself. The side taps are small and positive, adding just enough of the delayed and advanced copies to cancel the negative tails at ±1. Note also that we only forced two zeros; the ISI at ±2 is left untouched, which is the price of using only three taps.

4.14 Timing extraction

Function 2 of the repeater. The receiver needs a clock, and nobody sent it one — so it must be manufactured from the data itself.

In simple words — how you make a clock out of nothing

The received data already contains a weak hidden rhythm at the symbol rate — but it is buried, and in a bipolar signal the positive and negative swings tend to cancel it out. Each block digs it out:

  1. Equalizer — cleans up the pulse shape first.
  2. Rectifier and clipper — flips all the negative parts positive. Now nothing cancels, and the symbol-rate rhythm becomes strong.
  3. Timing extractor — a narrow resonant filter tuned to the symbol rate. It rings like a tuning fork and outputs a clean sine wave at exactly that frequency.
  4. Amplifier and phase shifter — boost it, then slide it sideways so the clock edge lands at the optimum sampling instant (the middle of the eye).
  5. Limiter — squares the smooth sine into a sharp rectangular clock.
  6. Pulse generator — turns each edge into a narrow pulse to trigger the regenerator.

This is why self-synchronising line codes matter. If the data has no transitions, there is no rhythm to extract, and this entire chain has nothing to work with.

4.15 Duobinary signalling

One last idea, and it is a clever reversal of everything so far. Also called correlative coding or partial response signalling.

The idea — if you cannot beat ISI, control it

So far the goal has been zero ISI: p(nT) = 1 for n = 0, 0 otherwise. But we saw in section 4.6 that hitting the ideal Nyquist rate requires an impossible brick-wall filter.

Duobinary takes the opposite approach. Instead of fighting ISI, it deliberately introduces a known, controlled amount of it, then subtracts it back out at the receiver. Your slide puts it exactly:

“In partial response signaling, the requirement of the zero ISI condition is relaxed as a controlled amount of ISI is introduced in the transmitted signal and is counteracted at the receiver side.”

The relaxed condition is p(nT) = 1 for n = 0 and n = 1, 0 otherwise — the ISI is limited to two adjacent samples. Because that interference is deterministic (you know exactly how much and from where), its effect can be removed at detection.

Formula — the duobinary encoding process
an=binary input bit,anin{0,1}a_{n} = \text{binary input}\, \mathrm{bit}, a_{n} \quad\text{in}\quad \{0, 1\}an​=binary inputbit,an​in{0,1}

2. bn = NRZ polar output of the level converter:

bn=−difan=0;bn=+difan=1b_{n} = - d \quad\text{if}\quad a_{n} = 0; b_{n} = + d \quad\text{if}\quad a_{n} = 1bn​=−difan​=0;bn​=+difan​=1

3. yn = bn + bn−1 =

+2difan=an−1=1+ 2 d \quad\text{if}\quad a_{n} = a_{n - 1} = 1+2difan​=an−1​=1
0ifan≠an−10 \quad\text{if}\quad a_{n} \ne a_{n - 1}0ifan​=an−1​
−2difan=an−1=0- 2 d \quad\text{if}\quad a_{n} = a_{n - 1} = 0−2difan​=an−1​=0

Decoding: b̂n = yn − b̂n−1

In simple words

Step 2 turns your 0s and 1s into −d and +d volts. Step 3 is the key: each transmitted value is the sum of the current symbol and the previous one. That sum is the “controlled ISI” — you have deliberately let one neighbour leak in.

The result is a three-level signal: +2d, 0 or −2d. And notice what those three levels tell you:

  • +2d → both this bit and the last one were 1
  • −2d → both were 0
  • 0 → they were different

Your slide makes the contrast precisely: the samples bn are uncorrelated (just +d or −d), but the samples yn are correlated — which is why the technique is called correlative coding. The encoding deliberately correlates the present input with the previous one.

The payoff, and the role of the precoder

The payoff is the box on your slide: “we can send 2B bitrate over Bandwidth B.” Duobinary reaches the ideal Nyquist rate of 2 bits/s/Hz — the thing that r = 0 promised but could never deliver — and it does it with a realizable filter. That is the whole point of the technique.

The precoder exists to solve one problem. Plain decoding uses b̂n = yn − b̂n−1, which depends on the previous decision. So one wrong decision would poison every decision after it — error propagation. The precoder's XOR-and-delay at the transmitter arranges things so the receiver can decide each bit on its own, breaking that chain.

Correction — the postcoder rule on the last slide

The final slide prints the postcoder decision rule as:

if yn < d, then ân = 1  ·  if yn > d, then ân = 0  ·  if yn = 0, randomly guess

As written this is inconsistent, because a value can be both “< d” and negative, and the rule gives no sensible answer for yn = −2d.

The rule that actually works is a test on the magnitude, which follows directly from the three levels above:

if∣yn∣ is near 2d→this bit is the same as the previous one\quad\text{if}\quad \lvert y_{n} \rvert\, \text{is near}\, 2 d \to \text{this}\, \mathrm{bit}\, \text{is the same as the previous one}if∣yn​∣is near2d→thisbitis the same as the previous one
if∣yn∣ is near 0→this bit is different from the previous one\quad\text{if}\quad \lvert y_{n} \rvert\, \text{is near}\, 0 \to \text{this}\, \mathrm{bit}\, \text{is different from the previous one}if∣yn​∣is near0→thisbitis different from the previous one

Learn the three-level meaning (+2d / 0 / −2d) rather than memorising the printed inequalities — then you can always reconstruct the decision rule correctly.

Exam tip — the story of this whole module in five lines
  1. A bandlimited channel smears pulses, so they overlap → ISI.
  2. Nyquist: overlapping is fine, as long as the interference is zero at the sampling instants.
  3. The perfect (r = 0) pulse achieves this but cannot be built → use a raised cosine with r ≈ 0.2–0.5.
  4. Check your work on an eye diagram; fix what the channel still ruins with a zero-forcing equalizer.
  5. Or invert the whole idea: allow a known amount of ISI and subtract it later → duobinary, which reaches 2 bits/s/Hz for real.
05 From third.pdf and sixth.pdf — Tutorial 4

Measuring information

Here the subject becomes beautiful. Claude Shannon asked a question nobody had asked before: can you put a number on how much information a message carries? The answer built the digital world.

4.1 The two questions information theory answers

Your third.pdf opens with them. They are worth memorising word for word, because they explain why the rest of the course exists:

  1. What is the ultimate limit to data compression? How small can I squeeze this file? → The answer is entropy, and it leads to Module 7.
  2. What is the ultimate limit of reliable communication over a noisy channel? How fast can I send through this hiss without errors? → The answer is channel capacity, and it leads to Modules 6 and 8.

Information theory is a branch of probability theory. It does not care whether your channel is copper or fibre or air — it is pure mathematics about sources and channels. That is why its answers are ultimate limits that no future technology can beat.

In simple words — the two building blocks

Your slides model everything with two idealised pieces:

The Binary Source (BS) — a machine that spits out 0s and 1s at a rate of Rb symbols per second.

The Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC) — a pipe that carries one symbol per time unit, but is unreliable: with probability p the bit comes out flipped. “Symmetric” means a 0 turning into a 1 is just as likely as a 1 turning into a 0. Normally 0 ≤ p ≤ 1/2.

4.2 What is information?

This is the idea that trips everyone up at first, so read it twice. Your slide says it plainly:

The key idea

Information depends only on the probability of the event. It does not depend on the content, the meaning, or the importance of the message.

A message about the least likely event contains the maximum information.

Compare two messages sent to you in Surat in June:

  • “It rained today.” — It is the monsoon. You expected it. This tells you almost nothing. Low information.
  • “It snowed today.” — Astonishing. You would call everyone you know. Enormous information.

Both sentences are five words long. Both cost the same to send. But one surprised you and the other did not. Information, in Shannon's sense, is a measurement of surprise.

The four axioms

Before writing a formula, Shannon listed what any sensible measure of information must obey. Your slide gives four. If you are asked to “justify the logarithmic measure of information”, this list is the answer:

Axioms of an information measure
#AxiomWhy it must be true
1I(p) ≥ 0You can never learn a negative amount. At worst you learn nothing.
2I(1) = 0An event that was certain to happen tells you nothing when it happens.
3I(p1p2) = I(p1) + I(p2)Two independent pieces of news should add up. Learning two unrelated facts gives you the sum of their information.
4I(p) is continuous and decreasing in pA slightly less likely event carries slightly more information — no sudden jumps, and rarer always means more.

Only one kind of function satisfies all four at once: the logarithm of 1/p. Axiom 3 is the decisive one, because the logarithm is the function that turns multiplication into addition.

4.3 The information content formula

Formula — information content of one symbol
I(xi)=log⁡b(1P(xi))=−log⁡bP(xi)I(x_{i}) = \log_{b}\left( \frac{1}{P(x_{i})} \right) = - \log_{b} P(x_{i})I(xi​)=logb​(P(xi​)1​)=−logb​P(xi​)

P(xi) = probability that symbol xi happens  ·  b = the base of the logarithm

In simple words

Take the probability. Flip it upside down (that turns “rare” into “big”). Take the log of that (which stops the numbers exploding, and makes independent events add). That is all the formula does.

The minus sign in the second version is not making the answer negative. Probabilities are always less than 1, so their logarithm is always negative — and the minus sign flips it back to positive. Both versions give the same positive answer. Use whichever is easier.

The three units

The base b only changes the unit you measure information in, exactly like measuring a length in metres or feet.

Units of information
Base bUnitWhen used
2bitThe standard everywhere in this subject. Assume this unless told otherwise.
enatNatural log. Convenient in theoretical proofs.
10hartley (or decit)Rare. Named after Ralph Hartley.
Exam tip — computing log2 on a normal calculator

Most calculators have no log2 button. Use the change-of-base rule, which is on your slide:

log⁡2α=ln⁡αln⁡2=log⁡10αlog⁡102\log_{2} \alpha = \frac{\ln \alpha}{\ln} 2 = \frac{\log_{10} \alpha}{\log_{10}} 2log2​α=lnlnα​2=log10​log10​α​2

Since log10 2 = 0.3010, a fast shortcut is log2 a = log10 a ÷ 0.3010, or equivalently × 3.322.

Worth memorising outright: log22 = 1, log24 = 2, log28 = 3, log216 = 4, log232 = 5, log264 = 6, log2128 = 7, log2256 = 8, log2512 = 9, log21024 = 10. Also log23 = 1.585, log25 = 2.322, log26 = 2.585, log210 = 3.322.

Four properties of I(xi)

  1. I(xi) = 0 when P(xi) = 1 — a certain event carries no information.
  2. I(xi) ≥ 0 — never negative.
  3. I(xi) > I(xj) if P(xi) < P(xj) — the rarer event carries more.
  4. I(xi, xj) = I(xi) + I(xj) if the two are independent — information adds.
Worked example — Tutorial 4, Example 1

Question. An event E occurs with probability p(E) = 0.2. Compute I(E) in bits, nats and hartleys.

  1. In bits (base 2)
