C Appendix

Test yourself

Try to answer before you open each one. If you can do all forty, you know this material. Answers are written out in full, not just stated.

Modules 1–3 — system, PCM, line codes

1. Why does source coding remove redundancy while channel coding adds it?

Source coding removes useless, accidental redundancy that was already in the data, to make it smaller. Channel coding then adds back a small amount of carefully designed redundancy whose mathematical structure lets the receiver detect and correct noise errors. You throw out the junk, then add the right tool. No contradiction.

2. What do the four letters of AWGN stand for, and what does each mean?

Additive — noise adds to the signal, y(t) = x(t) + n(t). White — equal power at all frequencies. Gaussian — the noise voltage follows a bell curve. Noise — unwanted random energy, mostly thermal.

3. A signal has bandwidth 8 kHz and is quantized into 256 levels. Find fs, n, Rb and SQNR.

fs = 2 × 8 kHz = 16 kSamples/s.
n = log2 256 = 8 bits/sample (since 256 = 28).
Rb = 8 × 16 000 = 128 kb/s.
SQNR = 6.02(8) + 1.76 = 48.16 + 1.76 = 49.92 dB.

4. Why does an RZ code need twice the bandwidth of NRZ?

In RZ the pulse only occupies half the bit period, so it is half as wide in time. A narrower pulse changes twice as fast, and faster changes contain higher frequencies. Since bandwidth is roughly the inverse of pulse width, halving the width doubles the bandwidth.

5. Draw AMI for the bit stream 1 0 1 1 0 1.

Ignore the zeros and number the 1s: first, second, third, fourth. Assign alternating signs: +A, −A, +A, −A. So the waveform is +A, 0, −A, +A, 0, −A. Zeros sit at the 0 level.

6. A channel of 100 kHz carries data at 125 kb/s with raised-cosine pulses. Find α.

Use BT = (Rb/2)(1 + α). So 100 000 = (125 000/2)(1 + α) = 62 500(1 + α).
Therefore 1 + α = 100 000/62 500 = 1.6, giving α = 0.6.

7. What is ISI and how does the raised-cosine pulse defeat it?

ISI is Intersymbol Interference: a bandwidth-limited channel smears each pulse in time so its tails spill into neighbouring symbol slots and corrupt them. The raised-cosine pulse is shaped so that it is exactly zero at every other sampling instant. Its tails still overlap in time, but they contribute nothing at the precise moments when the neighbours are sampled, so there is no interference.

8. A signal has r = 1 and a bit rate of 200 kbps. Find the average baud rate.

Use S = c × N × (1/r) with the average case factor c = ½:
S = ½ × 200 000 × (1/1) = 100 kbaud.

9. Name the four reasons we need line coding.

1. Baseline wandering — the receiver’s running average drifts on long runs of the same bit, moving the decision threshold.
2. Lack of synchronization — if the receiver clock is fast or slow it samples in the wrong places.
3. DC components — constant voltages create very low frequencies, which transformers and telephone lines (below 200 Hz) cannot pass.
4. Self-synchronization — the signal should carry its own timing, via transitions marking the start, middle or end of each pulse.

10. A receiver clock is 0.2% fast on a 2 Mbps link. How many extra bits per second?

0.2% of 2 000 000 = 4000 extra bits per second. The same 0.2% error on a 1 kbps link would give only 2 extra bits — the damage scales with speed, which is why fast links need self-synchronising codes.

11. What is the difference between NRZ-L and NRZ-I, and why does it matter?

In NRZ-L the voltage level gives the bit directly — it is absolute. In NRZ-I the bit is carried by whether the level inverted at the start of the bit — it is differential.

It matters because if the two wires are accidentally swapped, NRZ-L inverts every single bit and the message is destroyed, whereas NRZ-I still decodes correctly because the changes are still in the same places.

12. Why does Manchester need twice the bandwidth of NRZ — and what do you get for it?

Manchester has r = ½, so Save = N instead of N/2 — twice as many signal elements per second, hence twice the bandwidth.

In return you get a guaranteed transition in the middle of every bit, so the clock can never drift, and zero DC component. Perfect synchronization and no DC, paid for in spectrum.

13. How does scrambling differ from line coding and channel coding?

Line coding chooses the waveform shape. Channel coding adds extra redundant bits for error control. Scrambling does neither — it randomises the data pattern so long runs of zeros disappear, without adding a single extra bit.

It works because XOR undoes itself, so the identical circuit at the far end recovers the original stream exactly.

14. Why did serial transmission replace parallel over long distances?

Two reasons. Cost — eight wires cost eight times one. Skew — no two wires have identical delay, so bits that left together arrive at different times, and it worsens with distance and speed. A single wire has nothing to skew against. Parallel survives only over very short distances, inside chips and across boards.

Module 4 — bandlimited channels, ISI, equalization

15. State Nyquist’s first criterion in both the time and the frequency domain.

Time: p(nT) = 1 when n = 0, and p(nT) = 0 for all n ≠ 0. The pulse is tall at its own sampling instant and zero at every other one.

Frequency: ∑m P(f + m/T) = T. Shift copies of the pulse spectrum by multiples of the symbol rate, add them all up, and the total must be a flat constant.

16. Why can’t we use the ideal r = 0 raised-cosine pulse in practice?

Two reasons. It needs a brick-wall filter — flat to W then instantly zero — which cannot be built from real components. And its tails decay only as 1/t, so pulses from many symbols ago still contribute; a tiny timing error stops them cancelling and the ISI becomes catastrophic. The eye pattern for r → 0 shows this: the eye is almost closed and th/T falls to 0.32.

17. A channel of 120 kHz carries data at 150 kb/s with raised-cosine pulses. Find α and the bandwidth efficiency.

From BT = (Rb/2)(1 + α):
120 000 = (150 000/2)(1 + α) = 75 000(1 + α)
1 + α = 1.6, so α = 0.6.

Efficiency βrc = 2/(1 + r) = 2/1.6 = 1.25 bit/s per Hz. Check: 150 kb/s ÷ 120 kHz = 1.25. ✓

18. What are the three cases of sample rate versus bandwidth?

1/T > 2W — no function can satisfy the Nyquist condition; zero-ISI signalling is impossible.
1/T = 2W — exactly one solution, the rectangular spectrum (sinc pulse). Minimum bandwidth.
1/T < 2W — many solutions exist; the raised cosine is the typical choice.

19. Name the six things you can read off an eye diagram.

1. The optimum sampling instant, at maximum eye opening.
2. The noise margin — the vertical opening.
3. The slope — sensitivity to sampling time.
4. Level-crossing ambiguity — the timing jitter.
5. Distortion at the best sampling point — the ISI.
6. The error-free sampling region — the horizontal width.

20. Why does a regenerative repeater beat an analog amplifier?

An amplifier boosts signal and noise, so noise accumulates at every hop and the link degrades without limit — noise propagation. A regenerative repeater decides what the bit was, discards the noisy waveform, and builds a brand new perfect pulse, so noise does not accumulate at all.

Its one weakness: if the detector decides wrongly, that error is regenerated perfectly and propagated forward, and nothing downstream can detect it.

21. What are the three functions of a regenerative repeater?

1. Reshaping incoming pulses by means of an equalizer.
2. Extracting the timing needed to sample at the optimum instants.
3. Making symbol detection decisions based on the pulse samples.

22. Why is it called a “zero-forcing” equalizer, and what is its limitation?

Applying the Nyquist condition to a (2N+1)-tap filter gives an infinite set of simultaneous equations in only 2N+1 unknowns, which cannot all be solved. So we force zeros at just the 2N nearest sampling instants and accept whatever ISI remains further out. Hence the name.

The limitation follows directly: a 3-tap equalizer only cancels the ISI from one symbol either side. Anything beyond that survives. More taps means better cancellation and more cost.

23. Write the matrix equation for a 3-tap equalizer when pr[0] = 1, pr[1] = −0.3, pr[−1] = −0.2, pr[2] = 0.1, pr[−2] = 0.05.

Each row shifts the index by one, and the target vector is [0, 1, 0]T:

[0][1.0−0.2⋅0.05][c−1][0] [1.0 - 0.2 \cdot 0.05] [c_{- 1}][0][1.0−0.2⋅0.05][c−1​]
[1]=[−0.3⋅1.0−0.20][c0][1] = [- 0.3 \cdot 1.0 - 0.20] [c_{0}][1]=[−0.3⋅1.0−0.20][c0​]
[0][0.1−0.3⋅1.00][c1][0] [0.1 - 0.3 \cdot 1.00] [c_{1}][0][0.1−0.3⋅1.00][c1​]

Solving gives c−1 = 0.210, c0 = 1.13, c1 = 0.318.

24. Why must the timing extraction circuit rectify the signal first?

A bipolar signal swings equally positive and negative, so its symbol-rate rhythm largely cancels out and is too weak to filter. Rectifying flips all the negative parts positive, so nothing cancels and the symbol-rate component becomes strong enough for the resonant timing extractor to ring at and pick out.

25. What does duobinary signalling do differently, and what does it gain?

Instead of eliminating ISI, it deliberately introduces a controlled, known amount of it — each transmitted value is the sum of the current and the previous symbol, giving three levels (+2d, 0, −2d). Because that interference is deterministic, the receiver can subtract it back out.

The gain: it achieves 2B bit/s over bandwidth B — the ideal Nyquist efficiency of 2 bits/s/Hz — using a realizable filter, which the r = 0 raised cosine could never do.

26. In duobinary, what do the three output levels tell you?

+2d → this bit and the previous one were both 1.
−2d → both were 0.
0 → the two bits were different.

So the magnitude carries the information: |yn| near 2d means “same as before”, near 0 means “different from before”.

27. What is the precoder in a duobinary system for?

Plain duobinary decoding uses b̂n = yn − b̂n−1, which depends on the previous decision. One wrong decision would then poison every decision after it — error propagation. The precoder’s XOR-and-delay at the transmitter arranges things so the receiver can decide each bit independently, breaking that chain.

Modules 5–6 — information and capacity

28. A source has four symbols with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125. Find H(X).

The logs are exact here: log20.5 = −1, log20.25 = −2, log20.125 = −3.
H(X) = −[0.5(−1) + 0.25(−2) + 0.125(−3) + 0.125(−3)]
= 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.375 = 1.75 bits/symbol.
Check: maximum would be log2 4 = 2, and 1.75 < 2. ✓

29. Why is entropy maximum when all symbols are equally likely?

Entropy measures average uncertainty. When probabilities are lopsided, you can partly guess what is coming, so on average each symbol surprises you less. When all symbols are equally likely, you have no basis for a guess at all, so every symbol delivers the maximum possible surprise. That maximum equals log2 m.

30. A source with H(X) = 2.5 bits/symbol emits 1000 symbols/sec. What is R?

R = r H(X) = 1000 × 2.5 = 2500 bits/sec.

31. Why must every row of a channel matrix sum to 1, but not every column?

Each row corresponds to one transmitted symbol, and lists the probabilities of everything it might turn into. Something must come out, so those probabilities must account for 100% of cases — hence each row sums to 1. A column corresponds to one received symbol and collects contributions from different inputs; there is no rule forcing those to total 1.

32. A BSC has p = 0.1. Find its capacity per symbol.

Cs = 1 + p log2p + (1−p) log2(1−p)
= 1 + 0.1 log2(0.1) + 0.9 log2(0.9)
= 1 + 0.1(−3.322) + 0.9(−0.152)
= 1 − 0.3322 − 0.1368 = 0.531 bits/symbol.
So a 10% error rate costs you nearly half your capacity.

33. A channel has B = 4 kHz and SNR = 20 dB. Find its capacity.

First convert dB to a ratio: S/N = 1020/10 = 102 = 100.
C = B log2(1 + S/N) = 4000 × log2(101) = 4000 × 6.658 = 26 632 bits/s.

34. State Shannon's channel coding theorem and say why it is surprising.

If the information rate of a source does not exceed the channel capacity, then a coding technique exists that allows transmission over that unreliable channel with an arbitrarily low error rate.

It is surprising because before Shannon everyone assumed that cutting errors meant slowing down towards zero. Shannon showed you can run at full speed right up to C and still get near-perfect reliability. The catch is that he proved such codes exist without showing how to build them.

Modules 7–8 — source and channel coding

35. A code has H(X) = 1.75 and L = 1.80. Find η and γ.

η = H(X)/L = 1.75/1.80 = 0.972, so 97.2% efficient.
γ = 1 − η = 0.028, so 2.8% redundancy.

36. Can an instantaneous code exist with lengths 1, 2, 2, 3?

Apply the Kraft inequality: K = 2−1 + 2−2 + 2−2 + 2−3 = 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 0.125 = 1.125.
Since 1.125 > 1, the budget is overspent, so no such instantaneous code can exist.

37. Two students produce different Huffman codes for the same source. Can both be right?

Yes. Which branch you label 0 or 1, and how you break ties between equal probabilities, are free choices — so the individual code words can legitimately differ. What cannot differ is the average length L. If both students get the same L, both answers are correct.

38. A code has dmin = 7. How many errors can it detect and correct?

Detect: dmin − 1 = 6 errors.
Correct: ⌊(7 − 1)/2⌋ = ⌊3⌋ = 3 errors.

39. What is the code rate of a (15,11) Hamming code, and what is its r?

R = k/n = 11/15 ≈ 0.733.
Since n = 2r − 1 = 15, we get 2r = 16, so r = 4 parity bits. Check: k = 24 − 4 − 1 = 11. ✓

40. Why does Viterbi decoding use a trellis rather than a tree?

A tree doubles in size at every step, so after N bits it has 2N branches — computationally impossible. The trellis notices that the encoder keeps returning to the same small set of states, so it folds those repeated branches back together. The trellis stays a fixed height regardless of message length, which turns an exponential problem into one whose work per step is constant.

  • All the background the other units rest on: PCM and quantization, line codes, information theory, channel capacity, source coding and channel coding.

  • Unit 3: carrier modulation — ASK, PSK, DPSK and FSK demodulation and detection, and their error probabilities.
